initiatives.title: Front-of-House SOP, Training & Bench
initiatives.why: The clinic has no SOP for issuing letters to patients — medical certificates, referral letters, insurance reports, quotations. Nobody had ever said whose job it was, and that gap caused real friction between a doctor and the office. It is a symptom of a bigger one: a whole class of routine patient-facing admin has never been assigned or trained, so it defaults to whoever feels responsible, usually a doctor. The rule should be simple — the doctor supplies the clinical judgement, the front desk produces the document, the message and the follow-through.
initiatives.next: Write the letters SOP first (small, and it is the one that caused the friction), then the escalation matrix. Set the dates for moving Erincy to the front desk.
initiatives.gate: Capacity before capability — the desk cannot take on harder work while it is one person deep. Build the bench first, then load it.
initiatives.timeline: Bench Jul–Aug → P1 SOPs written Aug → ONE combined training block Sep–Oct timed to digital receipts go-live (#15) → P2 SOPs and first competency review Nov.

initiatives.title: Locum Payment Date — define & document
initiatives.why: Locum used to be paid on the 7th; it has been the 10th for three years. The office has been faultlessly consistent — the grievance is that the change was never explained. Moving back to the 7th costs the clinic about RM60 a month in working capital, so this is not a money decision at all. It is purely a question of whether the numbers can be known and approved by then.
initiatives.next: Emily logs the timestamps T0–T7 for the August, September and October closes. Decide 7th vs 10th with observed data on the table, then write it into the contractor agreement.
initiatives.gate: Set the committed date at the 90th percentile of observed completion, rounded to the next business day — not the average. A payment date is a promise; set it where it holds in a bad month.
initiatives.timeline: Measure the Aug/Sep/Oct closes → decide in November → into the contractor agreement.

initiatives.title: Supplier Register & Comms Takeover
initiatives.why: Supplier communication and payment should sit with the office, not the doctors — both to free clinical time and because doctor-mediated invoices arrive late. One supplier offers cashback for payment within about two days of invoice, and we routinely miss it because the invoice reaches the team after the window has closed. That is a pure, uncontested loss. Before anything can be taken over, we need to know the full universe of who we buy from and how each relationship actually runs today.
initiatives.next: Fill in the register: every supplier a row — who liaises, who gets the invoice, who approves, who pays, the terms, and whether the terms are documented anywhere.
initiatives.gate: Anything left as Unknown is itself a finding, not a blank.
initiatives.timeline: Register built and seeded. Fill it Jul–Aug, agree target owners Sep, hand over the relationships Sep–Oct.

initiatives.title: Supplier Rebates & Benefits Policy
initiatives.why: Suppliers give us more than goods — early-payment cashback, volume discounts, seasonal promotions, free units, sponsored courses. Today there is no rule about who those benefits belong to, which means every case is a negotiation. A rule you have to argue about each time is not a rule.
initiatives.next: Confirm the mechanics with the office, get the ethics position confirmed, then communicate it and fold it into the contractor agreement.
initiatives.gate: The benefit follows the cost and the risk. Whoever bore the thing that earned the rebate, gets the rebate.
initiatives.timeline: Draft written. Confirm the mechanics and the ethics position, then communicate.

initiatives.note: Cash-flow-earned benefits are the clinic's outright. Case-cost-earned benefits reduce the cost line and reach the doctors automatically — paying them on top would be double-counting. Personal benefits are declared and logged.

initiatives.title: Invisalign Invoice Verification — off the doctor
initiatives.why: A doctor personally checks every aligner invoice to make sure we were billed correctly. The right question is what she is checking it against — and the answer exposes the design flaw: she is reconstructing the truth at month end from knowledge only she holds. Verification belongs with the office, in line with the direction that all supplier communication and invoicing sits with management.
initiatives.next: Get the office read access to the supplier's case portal and the current price and tier agreement, then start a case log.
initiatives.gate: Capture the truth when it is created, not months later. The doctor confirms the case at the moment it is ordered — thirty seconds — and the office verifies the invoice against that log with no doctor involved.
initiatives.timeline: Access and price list Aug → case log running Sep → first office-run verification Oct. Automated matching later.

initiatives.title: AI Clinical Note Transcription
initiatives.why: Doctors spend real chair time typing the patient conversation into notes. That time is the most expensive time in the building, and the task is now genuinely easy to automate: record the conversation, transcribe it, and format it into the clinic's own note style.
initiatives.next: Get a sample of existing notes so the output can be matched to how the doctors already write. A handful of examples is almost certainly enough — no model training required.
initiatives.gate: Two non-negotiables: patient consent for recording, and the doctor reviews and approves before anything enters the clinical record. Never auto-write.
initiatives.timeline: Short term: a handheld device in the room. Medium term: a fixed microphone per surgery, with patients matched by timestamp against the appointment book.

initiatives.note: Run the model locally so no patient audio or clinical text leaves the premises — the privacy-safe answer and the easiest one to defend to the doctors.

initiatives.title: DSA Training Programme
initiatives.why: There is no structured training for the dental surgery assistants. The doctors already run a quarterly get-together where they teach each other what they have learned — the same model would work chairside, and running it is a real ownership opportunity for the senior assistants rather than a chore.

initiatives.title: New Doctor — capacity & case-mix hire
initiatives.why: Our own margin data shows a very wide spread in value produced per chair-hour between doctors — one clinician generates several hundred times the true margin per hour of another. Business as usual will not close the gap in time. A clinician who can arrive and immediately deliver higher-value procedures, and bring patients with them, is the case-mix lever — the only route past the capacity ceiling other than extending hours.
initiatives.next: Open the conversation with the candidate already identified.
initiatives.gate: Look for someone who can produce from early on, not someone who needs the clinic to build their book for them.
initiatives.timeline: Conversation now. Terms would ride on the contractor agreement.

initiatives.title: Recall Campaign Expansion — cold blast & post-visit follow-up
initiatives.why: The recall system was built with more triggers than the six, nine and twelve-month recalls we actually switched on. Turning the others on is the cheapest top-line lever available, and the P&L trajectory says business as usual will not close the gap. Messaging even ten thousand lapsed patients costs on the order of RM3,000.
initiatives.next: Amend the post-appointment follow-up message to also ask for a Google review, then draft the cold reactivation blast and de-conflict it against the call lists.
initiatives.gate: Do not launch anything while the recall link is broken — blasting the whole base into a browser security warning is worse than not blasting at all.
initiatives.timeline: UNBLOCKED 18 Jul — the recall link certificate is renewed (valid to 16 Oct) and the vendor has automated the renewal. Post-visit follow-up amendment first (fast, free), then the cold blast.
